item.title: Houthi attack on Saudi airport kills 12 including 2 Bangladeshis, over 300 wounded
item.description:
IRAN-CRISIS/SAUDI-AIRPORT

The third attack this week on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday left at least 12 people dead and more than 300 wounded, Saudi authorities said, as Iran-backed Houthis escalated the campaign they launched this summer against the kingdom.

The dead included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. At the latest count, officials said, 309 were wounded.

Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter said. Some were in critical condition.

Saudi Arabia says 3 dead at airports after Houthis claim attacks

Saturday's attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade, occurred without warning, with no alert issued by Saudi Arabia's threat warning system. This week's two previous attacks on King Khalid International Airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

The deadly strikes exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom's defence capabilities as it wages an air campaign against the Houthis to support a ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.

A Saudi-led military coalition vowed to respond to the attack.

Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have claimed hundreds of strikes on targets in Houthi-held territory. The Houthis have said these killed civilians including women and children. Reuters could not independently verify those claims.

All flights were diverted from Riyadh on Saturday, and operations at the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

The head of the Houthi media office said in a post on X after the attack that the group had "shut down Riyadh international airport". The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group on Monday.

US President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks, saying they "demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life."

Eyewitness saw wounded on the ground

One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing towards the facility. A video verified by Reuters showed ambulances at the airport.

An injured traveller told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.

The US embassy in Riyadh said it was "aware of attacks" and "strongly recommends all US citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas."

Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. The Houthis had stormed Sanaa the previous year, pushing out government forces.

The war was fought to a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. Saudi Arabia struck a 2022 deal with the Houthis, freezing the conflict.

That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces.

The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, which has so far made slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country's third-largest city, Taiz, under siege.

Riyadh due to hold major summits

Flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point.

Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences.

Organizers of those conferences said ahead of the strikes on Saturday they would go ahead as planned.

item.title: Rooppur nuclear power plant begins fission, moves closer to electricity generation
item.description:
The first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has begun a nuclear fission reaction, bringing Bangladesh’s only nuclear power plant closer to starting electricity generation and supplying power to the national grid.

The reaction is the process through which nuclear energy is released and marks a crucial stage in the final preparations for electricity generation and supply. The plant is scheduled to supply 300 megawatts of electricity to the national grid in December.

According to sources at the Rooppur plant, the process of generating energy through nuclear fission was initially scheduled to begin in September. However, the schedule was delayed after defects were detected during tests of safety valves. The valves were tested under high pressure in two rounds last week. After reviewing the test results, the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) approved the start of the reaction last Thursday. Nuclear fission began at 3:34pm on Sunday.

The Rooppur project in Pabna is the largest single project in Bangladesh’s history in terms of cost. The Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission, under the Ministry of Science and Technology, is implementing the project. The state-owned Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Limited (NPCBL), under the commission, is responsible for operating the plant.

Russian contractor Atomstroyexport is constructing two units at Rooppur, each with a capacity of 1,200 megawatts.

NPCBL Managing Director Md Zahedul Hasan told Prothom Alo that the final process leading to the start of the nuclear reaction began on Saturday after three days of preparation. The controlled reaction successfully started on Sunday.

“This brings to an end the long wait following the beginning of Bangladesh’s journey towards the peaceful use of nuclear energy in 1961. This is a major milestone for the country’s science sector,” he said.

Sources at the plant said the reactor vessel of the first unit had achieved criticality for the first time. This is a significant milestone for Bangladesh’s nuclear power programme. Following criticality, all key reactor parameters have remained within the prescribed limits, and the process is being conducted under controlled conditions.

Officials involved in the project said the start of the nuclear reaction was a major step towards connecting the plant to the national grid. The next stages will involve reactor physics tests, verification of safety systems, a gradual increase in reactor power and the completion of tests and preparations required for grid connection, in accordance with the approved commissioning programme.

Each stage must comply with the highest safety standards, approved procedures and regulatory requirements.

According to plant officials, achieving reactor criticality is not merely a technical success but also a historic recognition of Bangladesh’s capabilities in science, engineering and nuclear technology. After years of effort, the country has reached a crucial stage in connecting its first nuclear power plant to the national grid.

Reaction process likely to take 30 to 40 days

Sources at the Rooppur plant said a series of tests would be conducted following the start of the nuclear reaction. The entire process could take 30 to 40 days.

The reactor’s power output will then be increased gradually. Nuclear fuel fission will generate heat, which will be used to produce steam and drive a turbine to generate electricity.

Once the reactor begins producing energy, electricity can be supplied to the national grid when its output reaches 30 per cent of capacity. At that stage, the plant is expected to supply 300 megawatts of electricity, potentially in December.

Plant officials said trial operations could continue for seven to eight months after the initial start-up. Once electricity is supplied to the grid, Bangladesh will become the world’s 33rd country to generate nuclear power.

Rooppur was recognised as a nuclear installation after nuclear fuel arrived at the project site in October 2023. With the receipt of the fuel, Bangladesh also joined the group of countries possessing nuclear energy capabilities.
According to plant sources, once operational, the nuclear power plant will be able to supply electricity continuously at a steady rate, 24 hours a day.

The reactor will require refuelling every 18 months. A unit may remain shut down for up to two months for the removal of spent fuel, loading of fresh fuel and maintenance.

The sources said that once one unit of Rooppur became operational, it could save USD 1 billion annually in fuel imports. However, the project has already been delayed by three and a half years.

Project cost rises by Tk 260 billion


The Rooppur project was originally scheduled to run until December 2025. Its deadline has been extended twice, with the latest completion date set for June 2028.

Although the deadline has been extended under the agreement with the contractor, there is no provision to increase the project cost under that agreement. However, the rise in the dollar exchange rate has increased the project's expenses by Tk 260 billion.

The total cost of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant is now expected to reach Tk 1.39 trillion.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,162 as seven die in 24 hours
item.description:
Seven more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Sunday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,162.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all seven of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,058, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 104, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the seven new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in the Sylhet division with three deaths, while Sunamganj district recorded the highest district-level death count with two casualties.
A total of 1,180 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Sunday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 205,028.
During the same period, 93 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 22,421.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 182,047 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 174,469 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Bangladesh plans €250m investment in women's health
item.description:
Bangladesh’s planned €250 million investment in women’s health aimed to target approximately 47 million women and girls over five years, highlighted at the opening press conference of the World Health Summit 2026 in Berlin on Sunday where global health leaders gathered to discuss ways to build more resilient and equitable healthcare systems.
The Government of Bangladesh and the European Investment Bank (EIB) have set out plans to redirect the financing under an existing EIB sovereign loan towards the Women’s Health Initiative, which is expected to run from 2027 to 2031.
The program aims to expand access to maternal and newborn healthcare, cervical and breast cancer services, and emergency obstetric and newborn care.
It will also support stronger primary healthcare, referral services, district hospitals and critical care facilities.
Sardar Md Sakhawat Hussain, Bangladesh’s health and family welfare minister, said the initiative reflected the government’s commitment to building a stronger and more equitable health system according to a latest release by UNFPA.
“The health and well-being of women and girls are fundamental to Bangladesh’s future,” he said.
“This initiative reflects our determination to build a stronger and more equitable health system, one that prioritizes prevention and protects women throughout their lives.”
He added that the partnership with the EIB and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) would help ensure quality healthcare services reached communities across the country.
Dr Ziauddin Hyder, special adviser to the prime minister on health, said the investment would support a broader shift in the country’s healthcare approach.
“Our vision is to shift health systems from treatment to prevention and health promotion, and this new investment will help drive that national vision forward,” he said.
The €250 million program is designed to address gaps in women’s healthcare while improving the capacity of the wider health system.
Its key priorities include expanding maternal and newborn care, strengthening cervical and breast cancer services, improving access to emergency obstetric and newborn care, and upgrading primary healthcare, referral services, district hospitals and critical care facilities.
The initiative is expected to benefit approximately 47 million women and girls between 2027 and 2031.
UNFPA Executive Director Diene Keita said women’s health remained critically underfunded despite its importance to sustainable development.
“This landmark investment shows how national leadership and innovative development financing can combine proven strategies to accelerate progress at scale,” she said at the opening press conference of WHS 2026 on Sunday.
Keita added that UNFPA would contribute its expertise and longstanding presence in Bangladesh to help ensure the program delivered measurable and equitable improvements in the health of millions of women and girls.
“We need to shift the way we view women’s health: from cost to investment, from a niche sector to a national economic priority,” Keita said highlighting Bangladesh’s initiative.
She described investment in women’s health as an investment in a country’s people, productivity and future, adding that Bangladesh’s initiative could serve as an example for other countries.
The World Health Summit 2026, running from October 11 to 13 under the theme “From Crisis to Resilience: Innovating for Health,” brings together more than 4,000 participants on-site and tens of thousands online, with over 400 speakers across more than 75 sessions.

item.title: Dengue: Four more die, 2,193 hospitalized in 24 hours
item.description:
Four people died of dengue, and 2,193 were hospitalized after being infected with dengue in the last 24 hours till 8am on Sunday, according to a regular report by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
With four deaths in the past 24 hours, the death toll from the disease stood at 303 this year.
Of the newly hospitalized dengue patients, 1,030 were in Dhaka Division, 70 in Mymensingh Division, 293 in Chittagong Division, 304 in Khulna Division, 160 in Rajshahi, 84 in Rangpur Division, 236 in Barisal Division and 16 in Sylhet Division.
According to the report, a total of 99,275 dengue patients have so far been hospitalized across the country this year.
However, in the last 24 hours, 1,796 patients recovered and were discharged from hospitals.
So far, 92,803 dengue patients have recovered and returned home after receiving treatment in hospitals.
A total of 102,861 people were infected with dengue, and 413 people died from the disease last year.

Policymakers take on energy shock, rising debt at IMF-World Bank meetings
item.description:
Finance ministers and central bankers meet in Bangkok this week for the annual gatherings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, with the global economy buffeted between the US-Iran war's energy shock, rising debt pressures and the AI boom.

The meetings run from Monday through Saturday in the Thai capital, and will see policymakers tackle some stark choices, with the IMF calling on governments to rein in spending even as vulnerable citizens'' needs may be growing in the face of surging inflation and climate risks.

The week will see a combination of high-level closed-door meetings, public events and policy announcements from the world's top economic officials.
On Tuesday, the IMF will unveil its global economic forecast, along with detailed regional outlooks through the week, as policymakers set about tackling the challenges darkening the economic horizon.

In Bangkok, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva highlighted how the world economy was being pulled in opposite directions by the negative energy supply shock caused by the US war on Iran and the positive demand shock of the artificial intelligence technology boom.

"That shift into higher gear (from AI) is what is keeping the world economy growing at three percent," she told an event on the first day of the meetings, adding the growth was "despite the fact we are being dragged down by the energy supply shock."

At a press briefing, World Bank President Ajay Banga told AFP his message to developing countries on AI was to focus on building "small AI" applications, rather than trying to compete on capital-intensive models.

"Don't try and compete with America and China on frontier models and large data centres," he said. "You don''t have the computing power. You don't have the electricity. You don''t have the people."

Banga said AI-powered applications could run on less powerful smartphones and be used in healthcare, education, agriculture and other fields that are development priorities for low-income countries.

''Perfect storm''

Chief among concerns in Bangkok will be the economic fallout of the US war on Iran, which has seen energy prices skyrocket as Tehran''s retaliatory action has targeted Washington''s Gulf allies and curtailed global oil and gas supplies.

The IMF has warned that the effects of the shock have been unequal, with developing countries reliant on imported energy hit the hardest.
Despite the crisis, the Fund has called on countries to curb spending on subsidies and instead build their fiscal buffers after years of shocks since the pandemic.

Critics say that approach is just not feasible for low-income countries, and that multilateral lenders need to do more.

"The poorer member states of the IMF and World Bank are in distress from spillovers of the Iran war, rising interest rates in the West, and a climate crisis exacerbated by El Nino," said Kevin P. Gallagher, director of Boston University's Global Development Policy Center.

"The IMF and World Bank are not meeting this moment. They need an ambitious response that provides short-term emergency liquidity alongside longer term financing to make their economic growth paths less vulnerable to these shocks."

And the needs are great, according to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

The combined shocks "could leave millions more in poverty as developing countries struggle to sustain support for households," the UNDP warned in a report on Sunday.

"We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty," said UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo.

In the developing world, he added, governments are being forced to make the "impossible" choice between cutting support for their poorest citizens or risking their entire development agenda.

Advanced economies in Europe and the United States have weathered the storm from the rising energy prices better, but have not been immune to surging inflation fuelled by those price increases, which have begun to bleed into other goods.

That inflation has seen central banks around the world raise interest rates in an effort to curb rising prices, tapping the brakes on economic activity.
Still, advanced economies have seen a boom in investment in artificial intelligence technology drive stock markets to new highs and bolster economic growth.

The week will also see several key meetings on the sidelines, including of G20 finance ministers, where spiking bond yields will be high on the agenda.

A notable absence at that meeting will be US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who will skip due to "domestic engagements", a department official said on Friday.

item.title: Closure of Riyadh airport extended after deadly Houthi strikes
item.description:
IRAN-CRISIS/SAUDI-AIRPORT

Saudi authorities said on Monday they were extending the suspension of operations at the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, after deadly weekend attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.

Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to "allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities", the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.

The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.

The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East.

The airport cancelled 99.7 per cent of all scheduled flights on Sunday, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. An air traffic tracker from Flightradar24 showed no planes over the city.

The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia.

Lufthansa Group LHAG.DEhas cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM AIRF.PA has extended a previous suspension of services to and from the Saudi capital until the end of the month.

Abu Dhabi’s Etihad Airways was among the airlines that further extended Saudi flight cancellations, affecting around 20 flights to Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Monday and Tuesday.

The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia's real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6 per cnet this year, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity.

The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom's flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme.

Inflation may rise to nearly 11pc this fiscal year, IMF forecasts
item.description:
Bangladesh’s economic growth may slow this fiscal year, while inflation is likely to rise, according to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) October 2026 forecast.

The IMF projects that Bangladesh’s gross domestic product (GDP) growth could fall to 3.2 per cent in the 2026–27 fiscal year, while average inflation could climb to 10.9 per cent.

The outlook raises fresh concerns about the pace of economic recovery, people’s purchasing power and the investment climate.

The report was released this morning, Tuesday, during the ongoing joint annual meetings of the World Bank and the IMF.

According to the IMF’s World Economic Outlook, Bangladesh’s GDP growth is estimated to have reached 3.6 per cent in the 2025–26 fiscal year, while average inflation for the year is projected at 8.7 per cent. This means the country could face slower growth and mounting inflationary pressure in 2026–27.

Policymakers take on energy shock, rising debt at IMF-World Bank meetings

According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), overall inflation stood at 8.34 per cent in September.

The IMF projects global economic growth at 3.1 per cent in 2026, rising to 3.4 per cent in 2027. Global average inflation is forecast to stand at 4.7 per cent in 2026 before declining to 4.1 per cent in 2027.

Although the report does not provide an extensive analysis of Bangladesh, the IMF has warned in previous reports that slowing economic growth is a cause for concern.

According to it, weak economic activity can limit opportunities for fresh investment and job creation. In particular, if private investment fails to increase as expected, industrial production, business expansion and income growth could suffer.

World Bank report: Growth weakens, poverty rises, banking sector at risk

High inflation can also erode real incomes and purchasing power, placing the greatest burden on low- and middle-income households.

The World Bank recently painted a similarly challenging picture of Bangladesh’s economy, pointing to slowing growth, weak private investment and employment, and disruptions to industrial production caused by gas and electricity shortages.

According to it, non-performing loans and capital shortfalls in the banking sector are also increasing, while high inflation continues to erode people’s real incomes and purchasing power.

Meanwhile, despite substantial government spending on social protection, electricity and energy, and fertiliser subsidies, a significant share of the benefits fails to reach poor households. Many affluent families receive assistance, while some of the poorest remain excluded from social protection programmes.

World Bank-funded Tk 13b project to reform banking sector

These findings were presented in the World Bank’s October 2026 Bangladesh Development Update, titled Make Subsidies and Social Protection Work Better for the Poor, released on Tuesday.

The report identifies restoring stability in the banking sector, ensuring energy security and good governance, and increasing tax revenue as key areas for reform. It also recommends gradually reducing general subsidies while expanding targeted support for poor and vulnerable people.

item.title: 12 former advisers express outrage over harassment of Prof Yunus
item.description:
Former advisers to the interim government led by Prof Muhammad Yunus have strongly condemned the harassment of the Nobel laureate, expressing outrage in a statement issued on Tuesday.

A video showing Prof Yunus being harassed as he left John F Kennedy International Airport in New York in a wheelchair on Monday has gone viral on social media. The footage shows several people approaching him and shouting slogans in loud voices. The protesters shouted various accusatory remarks at him, including “Why you come here”. Several expatriate supporters of the Awami League, whose activities are banned now, have been accused of harassing him.

The former advisers issued the statement following reports of the incident. “We express our deep outrage and strongest condemnation of the continued harassment, online smear campaigns and orchestrated attacks targeting former chief adviser and Nobel laureate Prof Muhammad Yunus,” the statement said.

The signatories are former advisers Salehuddin Ahmed, Muhammad Fouzul Kabir Khan, CR Abrar, Asif Nazrul, Adilur Rahman Khan, Jahangir Alam Chowdhury, Sakhawat Hossain, Faruk-e-Azam, Farida Akhter, Sharmin S Murshid, Mostofa Sarwar Farooki and Syeda Rizwana Hasan.

In their statement, the former advisers said, “When our nation stood on the precipice of total collapse, the interim government led by Professor Yunus did its best in addressing the Herculean task of rebuilding a nation shattered by years of unrestrained economic plunders, collapse of democratic institutions and corruption, systemic tyranny and gross violation of human rights. It was this Interim Government that put an end to heinous practices like enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial killings that were regularly committed under the fascist regime.”

The statement said the interim government handed over power to an elected government following a free and fair national election in February 2026. The former advisers had hoped that efforts to rebuild democratic institutions, ensure justice for victims of the fascist regime and protect human rights would continue.

"​It is with deep regret that we notice that some political miscreants and a vested quarter are relentlessly spreading malicious and misinformation and physically threatening Prof. Yunus. We strongly condemn such cowardly tactics designed to create instability and undermine the credibility and wide acceptance of the interim government."

The former advisers said, “We state unequivocally: no amount of intimidation, falsehoods, online harassment, or personal threats will ever break our resolve for the changes July promised.”

The statement added, “​​The historic mandate of reform and dignity achieved by the people of Bangladesh and through enormous sacrifice of the youth cannot and will not be erased by malicious propaganda and attempts of an ousted fascist regime and its supporters."

Govt plans 81km elevated rail line from Dhaka to Comilla
item.description:
The Ministry of Railways has proposed building an 81-kilometre elevated rail line from Shyampur in Dhaka to Comilla to serve as an alternative route, which could reduce the rail distance between Dhaka and Chittagong by 80km and cut travel time by 1.5 to two hours.
Information and Broadcasting Adviser Zahed Ur Rahman disclosed the plan at a regular press briefing at the Secretariat on Tuesday to update the media on the government's activities. The information was also provided to journalists in a written statement.
He said the project's preliminary estimated cost stands at Tk83,901 crore. Construction is expected to take four years after land acquisition is completed.
However, he said the final decision on whether the entire line will be elevated will be made at the highest level of the government. The railway ministry has initially proposed an entirely elevated route, with the proposal submitted to the ministry on October 5.
The adviser said building the entire line on elevated structures would save around 322 acres of land. A combination of embankments and elevated structures would cost approximately Tk73,577 crore, while opting for a fully elevated line would add around Tk10,324 crore to the cost.
According to details presented at the briefing, the proposed line would support electric train operations in the future. The double-track broad-gauge railway would be designed to carry an axle load of 25 tons.
The line would have a maximum design speed of 160km per hour, while its maximum operating speed would be 140km per hour.

The top diplomats of Britain and Germany pressed on Tuesday for more sanctions on Moscow over its war in Ukraine, after President Donald Trump announced an easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel.
“I would say this is not the time to lower the sanctions regime but to strengthen this,” German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said during an event at the Warsaw Security Forum (WSF).
Ukraine and its European backers have been left reeling by Trump’s decision last week to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal to supply the United States.
The European Union on Monday formally added nearly 1,600 new Russian individuals and entities to its sanctions blacklist, with the aim of keeping pressure on Moscow.
“We are keeping our course,” Wadephul insisted, stressing that Europe was asking Washington to do the same.
Trump’s decision enables Russia to release large amounts of diesel onto global energy markets.
UK Foreign Minister Ed Miliband hailed the latest EU move and insisted on the need to “ratchet up the sanctions” further.
“We need to send the right message,” he told the WSF.
While criticizing Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel, Ukraine’s Western allies have all backed his unilateral declaration of a pause in attacks targeting the energy sector.
Russia has launched waves of attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure since invading in February 2022, knocking out power and heating to millions during winter months. Kyiv has, in turn, targeted Russian oil refineries.
“Let us take seriously this issue of the energy ceasefire that President Trump has talked about,” Miliband said.
He insisted, though, that it should not just be about oil refineries but “a broad energy ceasefire.”
Ukraine has only one oil refinery, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday.
“Last week alone we’ve seen 200 Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure,” Miliband continued.
“Let us seek with President Trump to hold (Russian President Vladimir) Putin to this full energy ceasefire because that is what we need,” he said, highlighting that Zelensky had agreed to the idea.
Wadephul also urged support for a full energy ceasefire, suggesting it should be broadened to cover attacks in the Black Sea.
Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II is nearing its fifth anniversary.

item.title: Economic growth to slow, inflation to rise, putting people under greater pressure
item.description:
Bangladesh’s economy could grow more slowly than those of other South Asian countries, while inflationary pressure is likely to remain the highest in the region.

According to forecasts by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Bangladesh’s gross domestic product (GDP) growth could fall to 3.2 per cent in the current fiscal year, while average annual inflation could reach 10.9 per cent.

There is little indication of a strong economic recovery over the next few years. The IMF expects growth to fall further, to 2.2 per cent in the following fiscal year. On Tuesday, the organisation published its World Economic Outlook, which included GDP growth and inflation forecasts for Bangladesh and other countries.

Sluggish growth will put further pressure on investment and employment, while high inflation will erode people’s purchasing power. The World Bank recently reported that around eight million people had fallen below the poverty line over the past four years. Approximately 62.5 million people in Bangladesh are at risk of falling into poverty.

Official figures put growth at 4.14 per cent in the previous fiscal year. If the IMF’s forecast for the current fiscal year proves accurate, Bangladesh will not have recorded such a low growth rate in the past three and a half decades. Its inflation forecast would also imply the highest average annual inflation in 15 years.

The strain caused by economic weakness is therefore not confined to growth figures; it is directly affecting people’s living standards. Weakness in the banking sector, energy shortages, stagnant private investment and shortfalls in revenue collection are making the situation more complicated. Taken together, these factors are fuelling concerns about economic recovery, job creation and people’s quality of life.

The IMF is not alone in projecting relatively weak growth. The World Bank and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) have also issued modest forecasts. The World Bank’s Bangladesh Development Update, published on 6 September, projected growth of 3.4 per cent in the current fiscal year.

Inflation may rise to nearly 11pc this fiscal year, IMF forecasts

Last month, the ADB forecast growth of 4 per cent. The IMF’s projection is lower than both. The government, however, has set a growth target of 6.5 per cent for the current fiscal year.

Official figures put growth at 4.14 per cent in the previous fiscal year. If the IMF’s forecast for the current fiscal year proves accurate, Bangladesh will not have recorded such a low growth rate in the past three and a half decades. Its inflation forecast would also imply the highest average annual inflation in 15 years.

The annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank are under way in Bangkok, the capital of Thailand. Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury met World Bank representatives there on Tuesday.

Asked after the meeting about the growth and inflation forecasts, he told journalists that the two institutions had issued their projections and that he did not want to dispute them. The government was working towards the targets set in the budget, he said.

Zahid Hussain, former lead economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka office, told Prothom Alo that, given the current trajectory of the economy, growth would be weak and inflation would rise to a high level.

Zahid Hussain, former Lead Economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka officeInflation must be brought under control and the obstacles to growth and job creation must be removed. These include a weak banking sector, energy shortages, disorderly budget management and inadequate social protection programmes. Reforms are needed in all these areas.

He further said the IMF, World Bank and other organisations were all saying that the country’s economy was going through a difficult period. Ordinary people were already under pressure, and that pressure would intensify. Inflation would reduce their purchasing power and push more people into poverty, he added.

IMF’s new $4.5b loan, deal may be signed in December

Growth could fall further

The IMF has issued forecasts for Bangladesh’s GDP growth and inflation, including projections for the next four fiscal years. According to its forecasts, growth could fall to 2.2 per cent in fiscal year 2027–28, below the rate recorded during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The IMF projects growth of 2.8 per cent and 2.9 per cent in the following two fiscal years, respectively, before it rises to 3 per cent in fiscal year 2030–31. In other words, the economy is unlikely to gain much momentum over the next three years.

In its report published on Tuesday, the IMF also provided growth and inflation forecasts for other South Asian countries, including India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. According to the report, India’s growth in fiscal year 2026–27 could reach 7 per cent, with inflation at 4.4 per cent. Pakistan’s growth is projected at 3.5 per cent.

The World Bank considers weakness in the banking sector one of the major risks facing Bangladesh’s economy. The non-performing loan ratio stood at 20.2 per cent at the end of December 2024. By June 2026, it had risen to 33.2 per cent.

Sri Lanka could record growth of 3.7 per cent and inflation of 5.4 per cent, while Nepal’s growth and inflation are projected at 3.7 per cent and 5.8 per cent, respectively. The Maldives could see growth of 3.8 per cent and inflation of 2.5 per cent, while Bhutan’s growth could reach 6.9 per cent, with inflation at 6.5 per cent.

What are the risks to the economy?

The IMF report did not provide an analysis of Bangladesh’s economy or discuss the challenges it faces. The World Bank, however, analysed the country’s economic situation in its Bangladesh Development Update, published on 6 September.

The World Bank report said several pressures were building up simultaneously. Economic growth was slowing, investment and employment were weakening, and inflation was reducing people’s real incomes. Weakness in the banking sector, energy shortages and revenue shortfalls were adding to the risks.

The World Bank identified weaknesses in the banking sector as one of the biggest threats to the economy.

The World Bank report further said poverty had increased because of factors including declining real incomes caused by high inflation and a slowdown in employment. Around eight million people had fallen below the poverty line over the past four years, while approximately 2.1 million more fell below it in the previous fiscal year alone.

According to the report, the national poverty rate has risen for four consecutive years, increasing from 18.7 per cent in 2022 to an estimated 22.5 per cent in the previous fiscal year. It could rise further to 22.8 per cent in the current fiscal year. Income inequality has also increased over the same period.

The World Bank considers weakness in the banking sector one of the major risks facing Bangladesh’s economy. The non-performing loan ratio stood at 20.2 per cent at the end of December 2024. By June 2026, it had risen to 33.2 per cent.

According to the World Bank, private-sector credit growth is at its lowest level in 33 years. Shortages of gas and electricity have forced many factories to operate below capacity. Some businesses have reduced working hours, suspended production or laid off workers. Foreign investment fell by 15 per cent last year.

The government has also had to spend several billion dollars more to import fuel. Meanwhile, revenue collection has made little progress. The National Board of Revenue (NBR) has been unable to meet its targets, with the revenue shortfall exceeding Tk 250 billion in the first two months of the fiscal year, July and August. These factors have combined to create mounting pressure on the economy.

Asked what should be done to overcome the situation, economist Zahid Hussain said inflation must be brought under control and the obstacles to growth and job creation must be removed.

These include a weak banking sector, energy shortages, disorderly budget management and inadequate social protection programmes. Reforms are needed in all these areas, he said.

item.title: Washington should provide Dhaka with increased support amid rising imports: Finance Minister
item.description:
Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury today, Saturday said Bangladesh should receive increased support from the United States in view of improving bilateral relations and the country's growing imports from the US.

He made the remarks while briefing journalists after a meeting with officials of the US Treasury Department here today.

The meeting discussed debt management, US assistance and overall Bangladesh-US relations, the minister said. He also held discussions with representatives of the US Export-Import Bank (EXIM Bank) and other US agencies involved in providing assistance.

"Bangladesh did not receive much from the United States in the past. But, as Bangladesh-US relations have progressed, we are purchasing several aircraft and importing oil, soybeans and various other products and commodities from the US. Therefore, we should receive additional support from them. They agreed on this. Now, let us see," Amir Khosru said.

The finance minister said the government's economic policy prioritises reducing dependence on loans and increasing foreign direct investment (FDI) and joint investment.

Khosru said he had held extensive discussions with the US EXIM Bank on the issue and expressed hope that Bangladesh could move forward with this approach.

"The main focus of our economic policy is investment. We want to move away from loans and focus more on direct investment and joint investment," he said.

Highlighting Bangladesh's substantial imports from the United States, the minister said purchases of aircraft, oil, soybeans and other commodities had implications for bilateral trade as well as Bangladesh's external balance of payments.

"We have strongly told them that Bangladesh is importing so much from the United States, and bilateral relations have reached their current stage.

If support does not come from the US now, when will it come? The assistance we expect should come now," he said.

Amir Khosru said the relevant US parties agreed with Bangladesh's position. However, he added, the extent and modalities of the expected assistance would become clear in the coming days.

item.title: Bangladeshis sent to Russia for jobs, used as 'prey' in war, 20 killed: SRB
item.description:
Thirty Bangladeshis went to Russia in search of jobs after being promised employment at construction companies.

But upon arrival, their passports and mobile phones were confiscated, and they were handed over to the military.

After 21 days of military training, they were deployed to the Russia-Ukraine war.

The Special Response Battalion (SRB) has found that at least 20 Bangladeshis died in drone strikes there.

A preliminary SRB investigation found that the Bangladeshis were sent to the battlefield as a kind of bait to identify enemy positions.

When drones struck them, the attackers’ positions and distance could be determined.

Additional Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Md Asaduzzaman, commander of SRB-10 Battalion, disclosed the information at a press conference in Karwan Bazar in the capital on Wednesday.

Two people have been arrested in connection with the incident: Mizanur Rahman, 55, founder of Jabal-e-Noor International and one of the key figures in the human trafficking network, and Abu Taher, also known as Lentu.

According to the SRB, the 30 Bangladeshis travelled to Russia on 7 May this year through three companies: Jabal-e-Noor, RS International and TS Group. Each was charged an average of around Tk 1 million on the promise of construction jobs. However, instead of providing the promised employment, the recruiters handed them over to the Russian military after they arrived. They were then sent to the battlefield following 21 days of training.

“The people taken from Bangladesh were not fit for combat. They had no physical, military or tactical training suitable for warfare. So why were they deployed after just 21 days of training? What we have understood is that they were sent to the battlefield as a kind of bait to identify enemy positions. When the opposing side launches drone strikes against them, its positions can be identified,” Asaduzzaman said.

The SRB said the Bangladeshis were deployed in three zones of the battlefield: the front, middle and rear. Seventeen were killed in drone strikes on the very first day. Three more deaths were reported at different times later. The battalion has provisionally confirmed the deaths of 20 of the 30 Bangladeshis.

At the press conference, Asaduzzaman said two of the survivors had returned to Bangladesh with injuries. One of them, Rajan, said a drone strike on the battlefield broke his pelvis and left the lower half of his body paralysed. He managed to reach a camp by crawling on his chest for nearly four kilometres.

Of the remaining eight, two are receiving treatment at a hospital in Moscow, while the other six are still on the battlefield.

Asaduzzaman said the trafficking network involved not only Bangladeshis but also a Russian national named Igor and a Kyrgyz woman named Julia. Efforts are underway to gather information about them and conduct operations. The authorities are also trying to arrest another member of the network, Mostafizur.

The SRB official said preliminary findings suggested that people from several countries had been recruited in a similar manner to fight in Russia’s war. From Bangladesh, recruits had come particularly from Gopalganj, Mymensingh, Narayanganj, Jamalpur, Pabna, Chapainawabganj, Faridpur, Rajbari and Gazipur.

Asaduzzaman added that most of the victims came from poor families, and some had borrowed money to travel abroad. Many of their families have now received news of their loved ones’ deaths but have no opportunity to see the bodies or bring them home.

He urged people to exercise caution when offered overseas jobs, particularly when making payments to recruiters, and to verify the legitimacy of the companies involved before travelling.

item.title: 2 major Bangladeshi conglomerates to begin lithium-ion battery production
item.description:
Demand for lithium-ion batteries is rising in Bangladesh as the use of electric vehicles and renewable energy continues to grow. Seeking to tap into this expanding market, two of the country’s major industrial groups, Walton and PRAN-RFL, have invested in the sector.

Walton will begin producing lithium-ion battery cells next month, while PRAN-RFL Group plans to import lithium-ion cells and manufacture battery packs at its own factory in November.

Walton Hi-Tech Industries, a subsidiary of Walton Group, has established a lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing plant in Chandra, Gazipur.

The factory will have an annual production capacity of 10 million (1 crore) battery cells. These cells will be used in products such as motorcycles, toys, rechargeable lights, rechargeable fans and digital scales. The company has invested Tk 1.13 billion (113 crore) in the project so far.

PRAN-RFL Group has established a lithium-ion battery pack manufacturing plant at its industrial park in Habiganj.

The facility will have an annual production capacity of 60,000 battery packs. The company has already invested Tk 250 million (25 crore) in the project.

Bangladesh’s annual market for all types of batteries is currently worth around Tk 150 billion.

Lithium-ion batteries account for Tk 20 billion to Tk 25 billion of this market. This means lead-acid batteries still dominate the sector. However, companies investing in the industry expect lithium-ion batteries to gradually replace lead-acid batteries.

Discussions with industry insiders reveal that demand for batteries is growing rapidly for battery-powered rickshaws, electric bikes and electricity storage in homes, commercial establishments and industrial facilities.

Bangladesh currently has an estimated 150,000 battery-powered rickshaws. The annual market for batteries used in this sector is worth between Tk 16 billion and Tk 18 billion.

Meanwhile, 12,000 to 16,000 electric two-wheelers, or electric bikes, are sold annually. The batteries used in these vehicles represent an annual market worth Tk 6.75 billion to Tk 9 billion.

In addition, batteries used for electricity storage account for an annual market worth Tk 9 billion. Companies entering the sector are targeting these three markets with their investments.

Industry insiders say lithium-ion batteries are lighter and more durable than conventional lead-acid batteries. They also charge in approximately one-third of the time required by lead-acid batteries, making them more energy-efficient. However, lithium-ion batteries cost nearly twice as much as conventional lead-acid batteries.

Walton to manufacture battery cells

Walton officials said the company would soon begin producing large prismatic lithium and sodium battery cells for battery-powered auto-rickshaws and solar energy storage systems. The initiative will require an additional investment of Tk 4 billion to Tk 5 billion.

Mahfuzur Rahman, chief business officer (CBO) of the lithium-ion battery project at Walton Hi-Tech Industries, told Prothom Alo that the company had completed the commissioning of the equipment installed to manufacture lithium-ion battery cells.

Trial production will begin this month or next month. The company also plans to launch lithium and sodium battery pack production lines within the next three to four months.

Mahfuzur Rahman added, “Using these production lines, we will begin manufacturing large batteries for easy-bikes, telecommunications equipment, IPS and UPS systems, solar energy storage, cars, electric bikes, forklifts and other applications.”

PRAN-RFL to manufacture battery packs

PRAN-RFL Group, one of Bangladesh’s leading industrial conglomerates, will begin manufacturing lithium-ion battery packs at its industrial park in Habiganj next month using imported cells.

Initially, the company will import lithium cells, along with certain specialised electronic components and other materials, from abroad.

As a result, local value addition in lithium-ion battery pack production will initially stand at around 20 per cent.

However, several senior officials of the group said it planned to increase local value addition to 70–80 per cent by expanding its own manufacturing facilities in the future.

PRAN-RFL Group said it would initially manufacture various types of lithium-ion batteries for easy-bikes, mishuks and electric bikes. The group will market these batteries under its own Blaze brand.

Asked about future plans, Kazi Rashedul Islam, deputy general manager of the RFL Batteries and Cables project, said, “We also plan to manufacture batteries for solar energy storage systems, IPS and UPS systems, backup power systems in the telecommunications sector, and energy storage at industrial facilities.”

He said the company planned to invest an additional Tk 1 billion (100 crore) next year to expand its lithium-ion battery manufacturing plant.

The lithium-ion battery plant of PRAN-RFL Group will initially create employment for 300 people. The company expects to generate jobs for another 500 people next year.

Although the group will initially manufacture lithium-ion batteries for the domestic market, it plans to export lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries in the future.

RN Paul, managing director (MD) of RFL Group, said, “Demand for lithium-ion batteries in Bangladesh has so far been met mainly through imports. In particular, finished batteries and the necessary components are imported from China. Once local production begins, imports of finished batteries will decline. This will save a substantial amount of foreign currency.”

Cabinet body recommends procurement of LNG from 5 suppliers
item.description:
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs on Wednesday recommended approval in principle for procuring liquefied natural gas (LNG) from five international suppliers through government-to-government (G2G) and direct procurement methods to help maintain an uninterrupted gas supply in the country.
The recommendations were made at a meeting of the committee held with Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury in the chair.
The Energy and Mineral Resources Division placed two proposals, seeking approval for LNG procurement under the Public Procurement Act, 2006, and the Public Procurement Rules, 2025.
Under the first proposal, the committee recommended approval in principle to process proposals submitted by Cheniere Marketing International LLP and Trafigura Pte Ltd for LNG supply through the G2G method.
The proposal was processed under Section 68 of the Public Procurement Act, 2006, and Rules 99(2) and 107(2) of the Public Procurement Rules, 2025.
The second proposal sought approval to purchase LNG directly from BP Singapore Pte Limited, Sahara Energy Resource Limited and Shell International Trading Middle East Limited FZE.
The Energy and Mineral Resources Division cited the urgent need to maintain normal gas supplies in the national interest as the basis for the proposed direct procurement.
The proposal was brought under Section 68 of the Public Procurement Act, 2006, and Rules 107, 97 and 98 of the Public Procurement Rules, 2025.
The committee recommended approval for the second proposal as well.
The recommendations are intended to facilitate the procurement process for LNG from the five suppliers. However, the proposals did not specify the volumes of LNG to be purchased, contract values or delivery schedules.

item.title: Pope Leo has cancerous tumour removed in lung operation
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV had a cancerous tumour removed from his right lung in a 90-minute operation on Tuesday and "woke up normally" after the procedure, the Vatican said.
A Vatican source said further tests were being carried out to determine if the cancer had spread.
"To ensure the procedure was radical, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed," the Vatican said in a statement.
The operation "confirmed the diagnosis of a pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the pre-operative tests", it said.
The 71-year-old pope was in the operating room at Rome's Gemelli hospital for a total of three hours and the operation lasted half that time.
"The surgery was successful and there were no complications," the Vatican said, with a source adding that he had requested dinner after the procedure.
Juanita Mora, medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association, told AFP that when this type of cancer is "caught in early stages, then it has a very, very good prognosis".
She said much would depend on the stage of the cancer found and whether it had spread.
In cases of surgical removal and when the cancer is caught early and localised, five-year survival rates from lung adenocarcinoma were "80 to 98 percent", she said.
"They'll determine if he needs chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy for the adenocarcinoma," she said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a practicing Catholic, said after the surgery that he and his wife were "united in prayer for (Leo's) health following his recent diagnosis".
"May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father," Rubio said on X.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said his "thoughts and prayers" were with the pontiff, calling him "a voice for peace, humanity and reason in our modern world".
Leo had entered the hospital smiling and waving earlier on Tuesday hours before the surgery.
He is staying in a room on the 10th floor of the building, next to a papal suite with a private chapel that is currently under renovation.
The Vatican has said it expects the recovery to take a week.
His audiences have been cancelled until October 20 and the operation raises questions about whether the pope will go on a lengthy visit to Latin America next month.
The surgery marks Leo's first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on May 8, 2025.
In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told crowds in St Peter's Square that doctors had discovered a nodule "at a very early stage" during medical checks.
"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene," he said.
The Vatican has historically been very secretive about the health of popes, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo's predecessor Francis, an Argentine who freely discussed his ailments.
Ahead of the operation, people outside the hospital expressed concern over the pope's condition.
Giorgia Fei, a 57-year-old Italian, said she had been worried.
"However, the Holy Father is in very good hands here at the hospital because we have some outstanding doctors," she said.
"I will pray a lot for him."
Giuseppe Purpura, 72, said he too was concerned.
"He's still quite young and I really wasn't expecting this. I thought he was in better health," he said, noting that "thankfully it was caught in time".
The Vicar General for the Diocese of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, led a rosary prayer for the pope inside the hospital chapel which was broadcast by the Vatican.
Dozens of people attended, and Reina asked all the city's parishes to join in.
The Vatican secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, told ANSA news agency that Leo had been "very calm" about his condition when they met on Monday.
The Vatican told AFP the nodule was found during routine health checks, and there were no symptoms that led to checking the pope's lungs.
Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is sporty and believed to generally be in good health.
He is scheduled to travel to South America from November 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

item.title: Modi's predicament: Gen Z pours out on India's streets as dissent surges
item.description:
Despite tens of thousands of security personnel deployed to stop them, youth protesters in India scaled barricades last week, chanted anti-government slogans and scuffled with police officers trying to drag them away.

“Long live the revolution,” shouted one young man before police bundled him into a bus.

Street protests in India this year are likely to be higher than at any time in the past decade, the independent Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) Project has said, as dissent mounts against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and Gen Z activists pour on to the streets.

Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014, with people under 30 making up nearly one quarter of the country’s 1 billion voters. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.

“The nation has suddenly found its voice,” said Yogendra Yadav, an anti-government activist who has played a leading part in the demonstrations.

“I would not say this is the beginning of the end of the Modi regime, but this definitely is the beginning of a downward spiral.”

The government and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party declined comment for this story.

The recent protests in the capital Delhi and elsewhere were focused on demands that Election Commission chief Gyanesh Kumar resign over a voter roll revision that activists and opposition parties say favours the BJP and has helped it win several recent state elections.

The ruling BJP, the government and the Election Commission deny the accusations. The BJP says the party’s wins have come from Modi’s popularity and strong economic growth.

But the demonstrations are also reflecting something larger: growing anger at Modi for failing to deliver jobs to millions of unemployed youth in his 12 years in power despite the surge in headline economic growth.

Other issues have also fed into the anti-establishment mood, including leaks of question papers in key examinations for jobs and education, the high number of crimes against women and the rise of billionaire businessmen alleged to have close links to Modi.

Modi has a strongman image and his government has previously cracked down on pockets of dissent harshly, but that hasn’t fazed the youngsters on the streets.

“The fear in us is gone,” said Ananya Raturi, a 21-year-old Delhi University student who was part of massive protests in the capital on Saturday.

Speaking after she clung to the windscreen wipers of a bus that police were using to detain protesters, Raturi said: “We don’t fear being detained or beaten up by the police. This generation enjoys it.”

Police have denied allegations that they beat up people at the demonstrations, saying protesters were handled according to prescribed procedures.

The rise of the cockroaches

The protests have been energised by the emergence of the first nationally resonant youth-led movement of the Modi era, the Cockroach Janta Party, which grew from online satire into a nationwide campaign this June after India’s chief justice likened the unemployed to “cockroaches”.

India’s mainstream media is mostly pro-government, critics say, and has covered the protests sparingly. But thousands of protesters armed with mobile phones as well as independent news channels on YouTube have amplified the unrest and made Internet stars of leaders like CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and firebrand left-wing activist Neha Bora.

Opposition parties that were subdued under Modi’s grip on power have been re-energised, with Congress Party leader Rahul Gandhi and tens of thousands of followers also on the streets.

The unrest has drawn comparisons with neighbouring Bangladesh and Nepal, where youth-led protest movements brought down governments in recent years, although analysts caution that India’s political landscape and Modi’s popularity make such parallels imperfect.

Many of the youth protesters grew up during Modi’s rise to power, buoyed by promises of jobs, opportunity and cleaner governance. A decade later, many say those aspirations remain unfulfilled and they say the Hindu nationalist government appears more focused on religious issues and divisive politics against minorities, especially Muslims.

The government has previously said the economy generated 168.3 million new jobs in the six years through 2024. Modi has repeatedly rejected allegations of any bias, saying his government works for all Indians.

30-year-old Gauri Seth, a medical student based in Kolkata, became a voter in 2014, the same year the Modi government came to power.

Seth said the Modi government promised “a lot, but has failed to deliver.” “Instead they focus on things like religious infrastructure. There are cases of violence against minorities. When anyone speaks against them, it is labelled as treason or sedition.”

It’s mostly about jobs

When Modi came to power, he promised the creation of millions of jobs each year. Yet, despite India’s strong economic growth since then, unemployment remains at slightly above five per cent, according to government data.

A Reuters poll last year said that data masks the severity of joblessness, especially among the youth. Unemployment among the 367 million people in the country aged 15-29 stood at 9.9pc in 2025, according to the data.

Research by Azim Premji University’s State of Working India 2026 report found unemployment among graduates aged 15-25 was nearly 40pc, while about one in five graduates aged 25-29 remained jobless.

In May, unrest erupted across the country when the government invalidated examinations for national medical colleges, a pathway to jobs for the poor and the middle class, after test papers were leaked.

Rubby Singh, a 30-year-old social activist in Delhi, said repeated examination paper leaks had deepened a sense among young Indians that the system was denying them opportunities even after years of study.

“This generation has been facing the brunt of not having proper education, which leads to not being able to get good opportunities,” she said.

While national elections are not due for almost three years, the country’s biggest state, Uttar Pradesh, goes to the polls early next year, which could provide a test of Modi’s popularity.

Analysts however remain cautious about the outcome.

The BJP may not be as strong as it was a few months ago, said Rahul Verma, a fellow at the Centre for Policy Research in New Delhi.

“But whether there are going to be electoral implications, it is too early to say.”

item.title: 103 Saudi-bound flights from Bangladesh disrupted, affecting 15,779 passengers
item.description:
Disruptions at various airports in Saudi Arabia have affected 103 flights operating between Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia on direct and transit routes. Some of the flights have been cancelled, while others have been suspended.

A total of 15,779 passengers on these flights have been affected.

The Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) disclosed the information in a press release issued at 2:00pm today, Thursday.

According to CAAB, 42 of the 103 flights were direct flights and 61 were transit flights.

Among the direct flights, 17 belonged to Biman Bangladesh Airlines, 10 to US-Bangla Airlines, eight to Saudia Airlines and seven to Riyadh Air.

Among the transit flights, 22 belonged to IndiGo, 14 to Emirates, seven to SalamAir, eight to Qatar Airways, six to flydubai, three to Air India and one to EgyptAir.

Until Wednesday, 100 flights had been affected, involving 15,393 passengers. The latest CAAB figures show an increase in both the number of disrupted flights and affected passengers.

Amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, Yemen's Houthi rebels have launched repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia. The deadliest attack took place last Saturday.

A total of 14 people, including two Bangladeshis, were killed in the attacks, while many others were injured. Following the attacks, flights from Dhaka to Saudi Arabia began facing disruptions.

Bangladeshi passengers travelling to Saudi Arabia have been facing difficulties as a result. Some passengers are trying to reach Saudi Arabia by taking flights to alternative destinations.

Biman Bangladesh Airlines initially suspended its Riyadh-bound flights and later suspended flights to Dammam. The state-owned carrier has announced that all flights from Dhaka to Riyadh and Dammam will remain suspended until 17 October in the interest of passenger safety.

Meanwhile, private airline US-Bangla Airlines has cancelled its Riyadh-bound flights until 21 October.

item.title: Load-shedding worsens in 21 southwestern districts, deficit hits 116MW
item.description:
Load-shedding has intensified across 21 districts in southwestern Bangladesh, including Khulna, with the power deficit reaching 116 megawatts (MW) during peak hours on Wednesday evening.
The shortage stood at 101MW during the afternoon, leaving residents grappling with frequent and prolonged power cuts.
Belal Hossain, a resident of Goborchaka in Khulna, told Dhaka Tribune that the situation had deteriorated compared with Tuesday.
“Previously, we experienced power cuts for an hour at a time. On Wednesday, outages lasted up to one and a half hours at a stretch. We are now facing 13–14 hours of load-shedding a day,” he said.
Ambia Khatun, a resident of Boyra, said frequent power cuts had compounded the hardship caused by the ongoing gas shortage.
“Gas supply is already severely disrupted, and we are trying to cope by using electricity. Frequent load-shedding has made the situation even more unbearable,” she said.
Latika Rani of Tutpara also reported a sudden deterioration in the power supply, saying outages often occurred even when electricity was urgently needed.
According to the central control room of the West Zone Power Distribution Company Ltd (WZPDCL), electricity demand across its 21-district service area stood at 694MW on Wednesday evening, against a supply of 578MW, leaving a deficit of 116MW.
In the Khulna zone, demand was 528MW, while supply stood at 447MW, resulting in a shortfall of 81MW. In the Barisal zone, demand was 166MW against a supply of 131MW, leaving a deficit of 35MW.
District-wise figures showed load-shedding of 29MW in Khulna, 4MW in Magura, 3MW in Narail, 11MW in Jhenaidah, 2MW in Chuadanga, 1MW in Meherpur, 12MW in Faridpur, 13MW in Rajbari, 4MW in Madaripur, 1MW each in Gopalganj and Shariatpur, 22MW in Barisal, 2MW each in Pirojpur and Jhalakathi, 3MW in Patuakhali, 2MW in Barguna and 4MW in Bhola.
At around 1:00pm on Wednesday, demand across the 21 districts stood at 661MW, while supply was 560MW, leaving a shortfall of 101MW.
In the Khulna zone, demand was 481MW against a supply of 422MW, resulting in a deficit of 59MW. In the Barisal zone, demand stood at 180MW, while supply was 138MW, leaving a shortfall of 42MW.
Afternoon figures showed load-shedding of 17MW in Khulna, 6MW in Magura, 1MW in Narail, 7MW in Jhenaidah, 1MW in Bheramara, 7MW in Kushtia, 10MW in Rajbari, 5MW in Madaripur, 3MW in Gopalganj, 2MW in Shariatpur, 25MW in Barisal, 3MW each in Pirojpur and Jhalakathi, 5MW in Patuakhali, and 3MW each in Barguna and Bhola.
The situation was comparatively better on Tuesday, October 13. At 1:00pm, demand across the 21 districts stood at 741MW against a supply of 705MW, leaving a deficit of 36MW. In the Khulna zone, demand was 567MW and supply 531MW, while the Barisal zone met its full demand of 174MW.
By 7pm, the overall deficit had risen to 79MW, with demand at 721MW and supply at 642MW. In the Khulna zone, demand stood at 551MW against a supply of 504MW, leaving a shortfall of 47MW. In the Barisal zone, demand was 170MW, while supply stood at 138MW, resulting in a deficit of 32MW.

item.title: Puja Udjapan Parishad reports 34 attacks ahead of Durga Puja
item.description:
At least 34 incidents of idol vandalism, temple attacks and other related violence have been reported at Durga Puja venues across Bangladesh ahead of the Hindu community’s biggest religious festival, the Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad and the Mahanagar Sarbojanin Puja Committee have said.
The two organisations called for effective measures to prevent further attacks and ensure the security of religious and ethnic minorities throughout the year.
The allegations were raised at a press conference organised by the two bodies at the Dhakeshwari National Temple complex in Dhaka on Thursday morning ahead of Sharadiya Durga Puja.
The leaders expressed hope that the festival would be celebrated peacefully and without disruption, stressing that religious festivals should unite people from all communities and reflect Bangladesh’s longstanding tradition of communal harmony.
They said they envisioned a society where Eid, Durga Puja, Christmas, Buddha Purnima and other religious and social festivals could be celebrated in a secular environment without fear or the need for police protection.
A written statement was presented at the meeting by Shubhashish Kumar Biswas (Sadhan), general secretary of the Mahanagar Sarbojanin Puja Committee.
Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad General Secretary Santosh Sharma said most cases filed over attacks in the previous year had resulted in punishment, with legal proceedings initiated and charge sheets submitted.
“This year, the notable development is that a total of 34 incidents involving idol vandalism, attacks on temples and other related incidents have been reported so far,” he said.
Sharma acknowledged that negligence by some Puja committees had contributed to a few incidents. Citing an incident in Netrokona, he said security arrangements had been maintained throughout the night, but no one was on guard at dawn when the incident occurred at around 5:00am.
He also said the temple's CCTV camera was defective and therefore failed to provide surveillance.
Despite these shortcomings, the local administration had taken appropriate measures, he said, adding that arrests had been made in 11 of the 34 incidents and action had been taken in the others. Some incidents were relatively minor, he added. “We are satisfied so far,” Sharma said.
However, he stressed the need for justice for major attacks against the Hindu community over Bangladesh’s 55-year history, citing the Ramu violence, the Nasirnagar attacks, the 2021 Comilla incident and the attacks in Sunamganj.
“Even today, we are demanding justice for all these incidents and exemplary punishment for those responsible,” he said.
Among those present were Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad President Basudeb Dhar, General Secretary Santosh Sharma, former presidents Advocate Subrata Chowdhury and Kajal Debnath, former general secretary Dr Chandranath Poddar, adviser Bires Chandra Saha, and Mahanagar Sarbojanin Puja Committee President Gopal Chandra Debnath, along with other leaders.
According to the written statement, incidents of idol vandalism and attacks on temples have been reported in several districts, including Sylhet, Rajbari, Panchagarh, Netrokona and Tangail, during preparations for the festival.
The statement also cited a theft at a historic Kali temple in Faridpur and attacks and looting targeting homes, shops and temples belonging to members of the Hindu community in Sunamganj.
It further reported a robbery in Naogaon involving individuals posing as intelligence agency personnel.
The organisations acknowledged that law enforcement agencies had acted promptly in several cases and arrested a number of suspects. However, they stressed that lasting protection for minorities could not depend solely on police intervention.
They called for a broader commitment to secular values and stronger social resistance to communal violence.
“Security for five days of Puja is not enough; security must be ensured for 365 days a year,” the leaders said, emphasising that building a discrimination-free Bangladesh required promoting secular values and ensuring justice for perpetrators of violence.
The written statement said the administration had assured organisers of full cooperation in holding Durga Puja celebrations nationwide. Authorities had promised adequate security, while relevant public service agencies had pledged support and assured organisers that any problems would be addressed promptly.
The Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad has also issued 22-point guidelines to its district- and upazila-level units to ensure the smooth organisation of the festival.
At the meeting, the organisations reiterated their eight-point demands to protect the rights and existence of religious and ethnic minorities in Bangladesh.
The demands include enacting a minority protection law, establishing a national minority commission and forming a dedicated ministry for minority affairs. They also called for proper implementation of the Vested Property Return Act.
The organisations urged the authorities to remove bureaucratic obstacles to the return of vested properties and restore ownership and possession of land to affected individuals within the stipulated timeframe, in accordance with tribunal verdicts.
They also demanded representation of minorities in the government, parliament and all representative bodies in proportion to their share of the population.
Other demands include enacting a law to protect debottor properties, or assets dedicated to religious institutions; passing an anti-discrimination law; and transforming the Hindu Religious Welfare Trust into a foundation.
